question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨3{x}^{5}+2y,\,3{y}^{2}-{e}^{x}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,1),$ and $(-1,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/26/269e3c7f92cee66c78f3226e7c967eb51153503c598d2e4d1e4b56a33e646ac4.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=3{x}^{5}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)=3{y}^{2}-{e}^{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=15{x}^{4},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(15{x}^{4}+6y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(15{x}^{4}+6y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[3{x}^{5}+6xy]_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(3{y}^{5}+6{y}^{2})-(-3{y}^{5}-6{y}^{2})]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6{y}^{5}+12{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{6}+4{y}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+4)-0 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+2y,\,{x}^{2}+2xy⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{2}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/91/9168d2ed7eeaa5f1dd331a0a986ac7ecfd6b964217a2cb614deb0cdd54437d65.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+2xy.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}4x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4xy\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{3}\,dx \\  & ={x}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & ={1}^{4}-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨6y{x}^{2}+{e}^{y},\,3{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/f6/f6e80e3010ec7c40d3f59dbb1da4e77c985c889a720b6f954177d8ad83a01351.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=6y{x}^{2}+{e}^{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=3{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=12yx,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(12yx+6y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}(12yx+6y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6{y}^{2}x+3{y}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6{x}^{2}+3x)\,dx \\  & =(2{x}^{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2})\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =22-0 \\  & =22.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
F(x,y)=⟨6{x}^{2}+2y,\,-10y-\operatorname{arctan}⁡x⟩

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(2,1),$ and $(-2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$

$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/3a/3ad0a876fe801980a2c3724a639fc6c379db750635c0278a10a5094e2d64c34a.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=6{x}^{2}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)=-10y-\operatorname{arctan}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=12x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-2y\le x\le 2y,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(12x-10)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2y}^{2y}(12x-10)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[6{x}^{2}-10x]_{-2y}^{2y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(24{y}^{2}-20y)-(24{y}^{2}+20y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-40y)\,dy \\  & =-40{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-40(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1},\,{x}^{3}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/00/006d80a7dbe4d03b78cc5fb1a642405e3fdfdd69ec9d80014ee8e0355ad1ae73.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{y}{2},\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y/2}^{y/2}(y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[x]_{-y/2}^{y/2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[\frac{y}{2}-(-\frac{y}{2})]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}+y)\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{4}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨30xy,\,15{y}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=y,$ $\,x=-\sqrt{y},$ and the line $y=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/24/24369439bc62cf06084a43d97dff0cee4e4089fd103511ef73d9dd5af1256ebb.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=30xy$ and $Q(x,y)=15{y}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=30y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =30y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):\sqrt{y}\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(30y+30y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}60y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}y[x]_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}\,dy \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}y(y+\sqrt{y})\,dy \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+{y}^{3/2})\,dy \\  & =60{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{2{y}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =60(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{5})-0 \\  & =44.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨14xy,\,6{x}^{2}y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e6/e6f6a5cf9b37fe16f17fe74face946d85b426badf8db710ca4a7ea308a1ff2ec.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=14xy$ and $Q(x,y)=6{x}^{2}y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=14y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{3}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(14y+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}(14y+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7{y}^{2}+6{x}^{2}y)\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7{x}^{6}+6{x}^{5})\,dx \\  & =({x}^{7}+{x}^{6})\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+y,\,xy+1⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=-y,$ $\,x=\sqrt{y},$ and the line $y=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/2e/2ecabe22395006f0c7ef0a3f914087fa324f4d59c7d7886c18907f824744643e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le \sqrt{y},\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y}^{\sqrt{y}}3x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-y}^{\sqrt{y}}\,dy \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
F(x,y)=⟨-x,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=-y+1,$ $\,x={e}^{y},$ and the line $y=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/72/728036ffc90e2476017b3102b6279f9c5900f0e7fc58536e76c9aa038eb04f02.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=-x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y+1\le x\le {e}^{y},\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{y}+y-1)\,dy \\  & =-{[{e}^{y}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-[(e+\frac{1}{2}-1)-1] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-e.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=\left\langle 2 x^{2} + 4 y, \; 2 x^{2} + 4 x y \right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{2}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/91/9168d2ed7eeaa5f1dd331a0a986ac7ecfd6b964217a2cb614deb0cdd54437d65.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 4 y$ and $Q(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 4 x y.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=4 x,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=4 x.
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq 1,\quad 0\leq y\leq x^{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds&=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx \\&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA \\&=\iint_D\left(8 x\right)\,dA \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{x^{2}}\left(8 x\right)\,dy\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left[8 x y\right]_{y=0}^{y=x^{2}}\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(8 x^{3}\right)\,dx \\&=\left[2 x^{4}\right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\&=\left(2\right)-\left(0\right) \\&=2.\end{aligned}
$$

D=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq 1,\quad 0\leq y\leq x^{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds&=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx \\&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA \\&=\iint_D\left(12 x^{2} + 28 y\right)\,dA \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{x^{3}}\left(12 x^{2} + 28 y\right)\,dy\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left[12 x^{2} y + 14 y^{2}\right]_{y=0}^{y=x^{3}}\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(x^{5} \left(14 x + 12\right)\right)\,dx \\&=\left[2 x^{7} + 2 x^{6}\right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\&=\left(4\right)-\left(0\right) \\&=4.\end{aligned}
$$
